clue.text: Subterranean and submarine deity

parts.note: the Roman god of the underworld is under the earth, and the wartime fuel pipeline under the Channel, Pipe Line Under The Ocean, shared his name

explanation.surface: A god who rules both below ground and below the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The Roman ruler of the underworld is the subterranean deity; the 'submarine' sense is the 1944 pipeline laid under the English Channel to fuel the Normandy invasion, known by the acronym of Pipe Line Under The Ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman god of the dead shares his name with the wartime undersea fuel pipeline, so both halves describe one name.

clue.text: America backs favourites without cover for Hermes

indicators.note: without here means outside, so the favourites go round the turned country

parts.note: pets are favourites, as a teacher's pet

indicators.note: America backs, so the letters of the country's abbreviation run backwards

parts.note: USA is the United States of America

explanation.surface: An American retreat leaves the favourites exposed, in need of a hat for the messenger god.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backs' turns USA to ASU, and 'without' (outside) puts PETS round it. The definition is Hermes's winged travelling hat.
explanation.definitionFit: The broad-brimmed winged hat worn by the messenger god in Greek art is his head covering.

clue.text: Dressed alike ? Odd, for I'm nude

indicators.note: odd means peculiar, telling us these letters come out in a strange new order

explanation.surface: A naked man finds it odd to be described as wearing matching clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd' rearranges FORIMNUDE, the letters of 'for I'm nude'.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldiers or staff in matching official clothes are dressed alike.

clue.text: Just the day for fruit under the greenwood tree

definitions.text: Just the day for fruit under the greenwood tree

parts.words: Just the day for fruit under the greenwood tree
parts.note: the gall that grows on the forest's typical tree gives its name to the May holiday marking Charles II's escape by hiding in that tree

explanation.surface: A fine day for picking fruit beneath the trees of the forest.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'fruit' is a gall growing on oaks; Oak Apple Day, 29 May, recalls Charles II hiding in an oak tree, and people wore such galls on that day.
explanation.definitionFit: The gall found on oak trees gives its name to the 29 May holiday, so it is both a day and a fruit-like growth.

clue.text: Their June samples were misleading

parts.note: the people who sample opinion before an election called the result wrong when the vote fell in June

explanation.surface: Someone whose June samples turned out to give the wrong picture.
explanation.walkthrough: The samples are not of goods but of voters: opinion-takers surveyed voters before a June general election and forecast the wrong winner.
explanation.definitionFit: Opinion surveyors take samples of voters, and a wrong forecast before a June election made those samples misleading.

clue.text: Aphetic novices are bound to work

definitions.text: Aphetic novices are bound to work

parts.words: Aphetic novices are bound to work
parts.note: aphetic means having lost an opening sound, so the word for indentured learners appears here with its first letter gone

explanation.surface: Beginners contracted to labour for a master.
explanation.walkthrough: Aphesis is the loss of a word's unstressed first sound; the indentured trainees are bound to work for a master, and the old shortened form of their name drops its first A.
explanation.definitionFit: Indentured trainees bound to a master; the old short form drops the opening letter of the usual word.

clue.text: Lincoln in the fifties always on the bottle ?

indicators.note: Lincoln sits in the fifties, between the two numeral letters

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral fifty, so two fifties give two of that letter
Abe is the short name of Abraham Lincoln

explanation.surface: A heavy-drinking President Lincoln in his fifties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts ABE between L and L (two Roman fifties). 'on the bottle' suggests drinking, but a label is stuck on every bottle.
explanation.definitionFit: A sticker giving a product's name is always attached to a bottle, which is the cryptic sense of 'on the bottle'.

clue.text: The old thing among the best people shows strain

indicators.note: the old thing goes among the best people, inside their letters

parts.note: saints are the best people, and STS abbreviates saints
res is Latin, the old language, for a thing

explanation.surface: An antique placed among high society reveals tension.
explanation.walkthrough: RES is Latin for 'thing'; 'among' puts it inside STS, the abbreviation for saints, who are the best people of all. The surface suggests an antique among the upper class.
explanation.definitionFit: Pressure or tension on a thing or person is a form of strain.

clue.text: One in nine brings back duckweed

indicators.note: the letters are brought back, so they read from last to first

parts.note: split as duck plus weed: a duck is zero, the letter O, as in cricket, and tare is a weed

explanation.surface: Someone among nine people returns with pond plants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'duckweed' is two pieces: duck (O, a zero score in cricket) and weed (TARE). 'brings back' turns OTARE round. 'One in nine' is one of the nine Muses.
explanation.definitionFit: She is the Greek Muse of lyric poetry, one of the nine Muses.

clue.text: Performers of hot " vocals "?

parts.note: vocalists are performers, and read another way, those who scorch things perform hot acts

explanation.surface: Musicians who deliver steamy songs.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks hint that 'hot vocals' is not jazz singing: people who scorch things are, read literally, those who singe.
explanation.definitionFit: Vocalists perform songs, and the word also reads as people who scorch or burn things.

clue.text: After the start, Pickwick's star sportsman failed to do so

indicators.note: the sportsman's name comes after that opening letter in the answer
the start of the word 'the' is its opening letter, taken on its own here

parts.note: Mr Winkle is the would-be sportsman of Dickens's Pickwick Papers, who boasts of his skill but cannot shoot or skate

explanation.surface: Dickens's famous sportsman, Mr Winkle, falls short of what was hoped of him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'start' takes T from 'the', and 'After' puts WINKLE behind it. 'star' belongs both to the sportsman's ironic billing and to the definition: what a star does, and what the hopeless Winkle never managed, is shine.
explanation.definitionFit: Stars glitter in the night sky, so to 'do so' as a star does is to sparkle or shine.

clue.text: Does this hunter buy places of refreshment ?

definitions.text: Does this hunter buy places of refreshment ?

parts.words: Does this hunter buy places of refreshment ?
parts.note: a shopper hunting cheap deals is asked whether, reading the name as two words, they gain bars, places of refreshment

explanation.surface: A question about whether a certain hunter goes around buying pubs.
explanation.walkthrough: The hunter is the shopper after cheap deals; split the answer as BAR GAIN and it suggests getting hold of bars, the places of refreshment.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheap deal is what a sales-hunting shopper seeks, and the word splits into bars plus gain.

clue.text: A chancy business when this vessel reverses

indicators.note: the vessel reverses, so the gambling word is read from its last letter to its first

parts.note: the football pools, a British betting game on match results, are a chancy business

explanation.surface: A risky venture follows when a ship goes backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: The football POOLS are a British weekly bet on match results; 'reverses' turns POOLS round. The surface makes 'reverses' a ship backing water.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-masted sailing boat with a fore-and-aft rig is a small vessel of this type.

clue.text: To which a blind eye was turned on a naval occasion ?

definitions.text: To which a blind eye was turned on a naval occasion ?

parts.words: To which a blind eye was turned on a naval occasion ?
parts.note: at the Battle of Copenhagen in 1801 Nelson raised his spyglass to his blind eye so as not to see the signal to withdraw

explanation.surface: An instrument someone deliberately ignored during a sea battle.
explanation.walkthrough: At Copenhagen in 1801 Nelson, ordered to break off, put his spyglass to his blind eye and said he saw no signal: the origin of 'turning a blind eye'.
explanation.definitionFit: Nelson's spyglass was the instrument he lifted to his blind eye at Copenhagen, giving the idiom of ignoring something.

clue.text: Simon's lack of complexes

parts.note: the nursery-rhyme figure is Simple Simon, so the quality he stands for is plainness, a lack of complication

explanation.surface: A man called Simon is untroubled by psychological hang-ups.
explanation.walkthrough: 'complexes' suggests psychology, but it means complications: the nursery rhyme's Simple Simon is the model of plainness.
explanation.definitionFit: Plainness, being without complication, is the quality the nursery rhyme gives Simple Simon.

clue.text: It's designed to be a bit of a cynosure

definitions.text: It's designed to be a bit of a cynosure

parts.words: It's designed to be a bit of a cynosure
parts.note: cynosure comes from Greek for dog's tail, and a decorative end ornament in a book is designed to catch the eye

explanation.surface: Something intended to draw all eyes.
explanation.walkthrough: A cynosure is a centre of attention; the word comes from Greek kunosoura, 'dog's tail', so part of it is a tail. A printer's end decoration is designed to be eye-catching.
explanation.definitionFit: A decorative ornament at the end of a chapter is designed to catch the eye, and 'cynosure' literally holds a dog's tail.

clue.text: More's mark

parts.note: the arithmetic sign meaning 'more' or addition, read as if it were the signature of Sir Thomas More

explanation.surface: The signature of Sir Thomas More.
explanation.walkthrough: 'More' looks like Sir Thomas More, but it is the word 'more', and its mark is the addition sign +.
explanation.definitionFit: The addition sign is the written symbol meaning 'and more', the cross used in arithmetic.

clue.text: "Alone and palely ——" (Keats)

parts.note: the missing word completes a line of Keats's ballad La Belle Dame sans Merci about the knight-at-arms

explanation.surface: A line of Keats with its last word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill in the gap: in La Belle Dame sans Merci the knight-at-arms is found 'Alone and palely' lingering, idling about.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats's knight is found idling about by the lake, the word completing the line of the ballad.

clue.text: Beyond words, this symphony?

parts.note: past means beyond, as in going past a place
oral means spoken, in words

explanation.surface: A symphony so moving it lies beyond words.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beyond words' looks like praise of the music, but it gives PAST and ORAL. The symphony is Beethoven's Sixth, named for the countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: Beethoven's Sixth Symphony is called the Pastoral, after its rural scenes.

clue.text: How you escape greeting the old bird

indicators.note: the words How and you escape, leaving the greeting without them

parts.note: the formal greeting 'How do you do' on meeting someone
these two words are the ones that leave the greeting

explanation.surface: A guide to avoiding the old bird when it says hello.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the greeting 'How do you do' and let 'How' and 'you' escape: what remains is 'do do'.
explanation.definitionFit: The flightless Mauritius bird died out in the seventeenth century, so it is a bird of old.

clue.text: Hang it ! Better try Battersea

explanation.surface: An exasperated owner told to try the famous dogs' home.
explanation.walkthrough: Battersea Dogs Home in London takes in lost dogs, so it is where to look if your dog has gone.
explanation.definitionFit: An American exclamation of annoyance, like 'darn it'; and, read as two words, the state of a lost pet that might turn up at Battersea Dogs Home.

clue.text: Not that the 'umble Uriah really lacked it

definitions.text: Not that the 'umble Uriah really lacked it

parts.words: Not that the 'umble Uriah really lacked it
parts.note: Uriah Heep in David Copperfield drops his h's, so he lacks the breathed h sound, yet he was full of ambition

explanation.surface: Dickens's falsely humble clerk was not really short of something.
explanation.walkthrough: Uriah Heep in David Copperfield calls himself ''umble', dropping the h; the word means both the breathed h sound he lacks and the ambition he had in plenty.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both the breathed h sound of speech and ambition, and Heep lacked the first but not the second.

clue.text: Born good among the trees

parts.note: ne, from French nee, means born, used before a maiden name
moral means good, virtuous

explanation.surface: A child born good in the woods.
explanation.walkthrough: NE is née, 'born', as used before a married woman's maiden name.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means of or living in woods and groves, so among the trees.

clue.text: Search out narrow ribbon

explanation.surface: Look for a thin strip of tape.
explanation.definitionFit: To rummage about and find out, as the hunting animal does; and a narrow tape of silk or cotton used for binding.

clue.text: Race Dad for a drink ?

parts.note: a race is a root of ginger, the spice
pop is an informal word for father

explanation.surface: A father in a running race for a beverage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Race' suggests running, but a race is a root of ginger (root ginger is also called race ginger).
explanation.definitionFit: A sweet fizzy ginger-flavoured soft drink, an old name for ginger beer.

clue.text: By inference, a female pawner?

parts.note: the pawnbroker is called 'uncle' in slang, so the woman related to him by inference would be his brother's or sister's daughter

explanation.surface: A woman who pawns things, inferred from the evidence.
explanation.walkthrough: The pawnbroker is called 'uncle' in old slang; so by inference a female relative of an uncle, a pawner, is his brother's or sister's daughter.
explanation.definitionFit: A brother's or sister's daughter is the female relation of an uncle, the slang name for a pawnbroker.

clue.text: Does the piebald horse drink nothing ?

parts.note: a pint is a drink, especially of beer
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A question whether the patchy horse goes without a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks if the horse drinks nothing; the pieces are a pint and O for nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: The American name for a horse with patches of white and another colour, a piebald or skewbald.

clue.text: A bit of hot stuff

parts.note: a fixed unit of heat, as gas used to be billed by in Britain, is literally a measured bit of hot stuff

explanation.surface: An attractive person described as a bit of hot stuff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hot stuff' is slang for someone attractive, but the bit is a unit of heat: British gas bills were once charged by it.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a unit of heat, 100,000 British thermal units, once used for charging gas supply.

clue.text: Exceed the limit with low scoring rate at Lord's ?

explanation.surface: Going too far by scoring too slowly at the home of cricket.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord's is the London cricket ground; in cricket an over is six balls, so one run in an over is a very low scoring rate.
explanation.definitionFit: To go beyond a set time or limit, and, read as two words, a single run scored in a cricket over of six balls.

clue.text: A bit previous, isn't it ?

parts.note: 'a bit previous' is slang for too soon, and the question asks whether the thing came before now

explanation.surface: A remark that someone has acted rather too soon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'previous' is British slang for premature; the clue reads as a tag question asking whether something happened before.
explanation.definitionFit: Something previous came before, at a sooner time, which is the comparative of 'soon in time'.

clue.text: Conductor for the chosen when they were transported

parts.note: the elect are those chosen, as by God for salvation
rode is the past tense of ride, being carried along

explanation.surface: A conductor arranging travel for a select group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conductor' looks like someone in charge of an orchestra or bus, but it is an electrical conductor through which current passes.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the terminal through which electricity enters or leaves a cell or circuit, conducting current.

clue.text: Loyal about an F.B.I. man within the law

indicators.note: the loyal word goes about the agent's letter, holding it inside

parts.note: leal is an old Scots word for loyal
a G-man is an American federal agent, so the letter G stands for one

explanation.surface: A faithful federal agent who keeps to the rules.
explanation.walkthrough: LEAL is Scots for loyal; 'about' puts it round G, from G-man, American slang for an F.B.I. agent.
explanation.definitionFit: Permitted by statute, so allowed and lawful.
